meta.description: Learn Aethyr by doing: short, story-driven tutorials covering the tools game developers reach for most: reading Blueprints, editing, batches, data tables, widgets, behavior trees, materials, the running editor, source control, and updates.

article.heading: Learn it by asking.
article.lead: Nineteen short stories, each a real thing you'd want to do: the exact sentence you'd say to your AI, and what Aethyr does under the hood. No tool memorization required, that's the whole point. Want one-line incantations instead? See the spellbook.

note.html: Get the samples first. Most of these stories run on the Aethyr sample content. Ask your assistant: "Install the Aethyr samples." It builds them into /Game/AethyrSamples and never overwrites your own assets. Run it again any time, because anything that already exists is skipped. A few stories (the project tour, the cleanup, the update check) use made-up /Game/MyGame paths since no sample covers them. Swap in your own assets there.

sections.heading: ① Read my Blueprint
sections.html:
You opened a project and there's a BP_Enemy nobody documented. Instead of clicking through every graph, ask.

youWhat does /Game/AethyrSamples/AI/BP_Enemy do? Give me the gist, then the event graph.
Aethyr · your AI BP_Enemy (parent: Character), 5 variables, 2 functions. TakeDamage(Amount) subtracts from Health and calls Die once it reaches zero. BeginPlay only prints a greeting. Here's the event graph topology…
used list_blueprints → summarize_blueprint → get_graph

Want a whole folder at once? Hand it to the audit agent:

youAudit /Game/AethyrSamples/AI: which Blueprints override BeginPlay, and are any variables unused?
aethyr-bp-audit agent Scanned 3 Blueprints. 2 override BeginPlay (BP_Enemy and BP_Turret). BP_Turret has 2 variables never read (Range and bCanFire), and BP_Boss never reads its ArmorValue…
a read-only fan-out: nothing was modified

Reads can't change anything, so this is the safest way to start. No need to enable writes. Great for code review and onboarding.

sections.heading: ② Say it, don't wire it
sections.html:
You want a dash. You could place the nodes by hand… or describe it.

youGive the player a Dash: a function that adds a forward impulse, with a 2-second cooldown so it can't be spammed.
Aethyr · your AI Added bCanDash (bool) and DashCooldown (float = 2.0). Created a Dash function: guards on bCanDash, applies AddImpulse along the actor forward vector, then clears the flag and re-enables it on a 2s timer. Compiled clean.
used add_variable ×2 → add_function → add_node → wire_pins → set_pin_default → compile_function

Under the hood: with the aethyr-edit skill installed, your AI assembles the whole function as one unit and runs compile_function to confirm it builds, so you get a working node graph, not a pile of disconnected nodes.

sections.heading: ③ All or nothing
sections.html:
Renames and restructures are where things break. Make the AI do it as a single transaction that either fully lands or fully reverts.

youRename Health to CurrentHealth, add a MaxHealth float, and clamp damage against it, all as one atomic change. Preview it first.
Aethyr · your AI Here's the dry run: 1 rename, 1 new variable, 2 rewired nodes, 1 clamp inserted, no conflicts. Apply it?
used preview_ops (nothing written yet)
youApply.
Aethyr · your AI Applied as one batch, compiled, saved, backed up. If the clamp had failed to compile, the rename would have rolled back too, so your graph is never left half-done.
used apply_ops (atomic:true) → rolled-forward, backup written

Why preview? preview_ops is a read-only dry run: it tells you exactly what a batch will touch before a single byte is written. The aethyr-edit skill teaches the AI to always offer it for multi-step edits.

sections.heading: ④ When the ritual fails
sections.html:
Errors happen. With the aethyr-triage skill, they're legible instead of cryptic.

youThat returned AssetNotFound: /Game/AethyrSamples/AI/BP_Enemy.BP_Enemy. What went wrong?
aethyr-triage · your AI You passed an object path. Aethyr addresses assets by package path. Drop the .BP_Enemy suffix → /Game/AethyrSamples/AI/BP_Enemy. Re-running now… found it, 5 variables. (If a name's just close, the error lists the real ones so you can pick.)
no asset touched: failed calls are side-effect-free

Every error names what it tried, why it failed, and the closest valid value. A failed write makes no change, so you can always just fix the input and re-ask.

sections.heading: ⑤ Summon a working pickup
sections.html:
The sample pickup has a body and no behavior: a mesh, a trigger sphere and a heal amount. By the end of this exchange it heals on touch, compiled clean, just from describing it.

youLook at /Game/AethyrSamples/Items/BP_HealthPickup. What's in it so far?
Aethyr · your AI An Actor Blueprint with two components: Mesh, a static mesh set to the engine's basic sphere, and Trigger, a sphere under it with SphereRadius 96. One variable, HealAmount, a float that's editable per instance, default 25.0. There's no overlap handler yet, so touching it does nothing.
used summarize_blueprint → get_components → list_variables
youNow the behavior: when something overlaps the trigger, heal it by HealAmount. Build the whole handler in one go and prove it compiles before you save.
aethyr-edit · your AI Let me stage it first so you can see the shape before anything touches disk. The handler binds the Trigger begin-overlap event, reads HealAmount, and calls a heal on the overlapping actor along with the wiring between them.
used compile_function (pseudocode → node graph) → preview_ops
youLooks right. Commit it.
aethyr-edit · your AI Applied as one unit. The begin-overlap handler fires on the Trigger, pulls HealAmount, and heals the overlapping actor by that value. Backed up the on-disk asset before the first save, compiled, and confirmed: 0 errors, 0 warnings. BP_HealthPickup now has a working graph on top of its mesh, trigger and tunable heal.
used apply_ops → get_compile_status

Under the hood: the whole handler went in as one apply_ops batch wrapped in a single undo transaction. Either every node and wire lands together or none does, so the graph never sits half-built between calls.

Look before you leap: preview_ops renders the exact changes without writing a byte, and compile_function assembles the graph from plain pseudocode so you confirm it builds before it ever reaches the asset. Reads like get_compile_status are free to call as often as you like within a turn.

Safety net: batches pass a compile gate before they save, and single writes save as they go. Either way the existing .uasset is copied to a timestamped backup before the first save of the session. If a change goes wrong, restore the backup over the file while no editor holds it. Reads never mutate anything.

sections.heading: ⑥ Onboard to a project you've never opened
sections.html:
You just cloned a UE project you have never seen, so map its shape without clicking through a hundred assets and without touching a single byte.

youI just pulled this repo and I have never opened it. What am I even looking at? Don't change anything.
Aethyr · your AI Read the project file. It's MyGame, editor default map /Game/MyGame/Maps/L_Startup, game default /Game/MyGame/Maps/L_Arena. Enabled plugins of note: GameplayAbilities, ModularGameplay, CommonUI, and a project plugin MyGameCore. Nothing here writes, this is pure metadata off the .uproject.
used get_project_metadata
youGood. Show me the Blueprints, and the AI ones especially. Then tell me what the big ones actually do.
Aethyr · your AI Under /Game there are 47 Blueprints. /Game/MyGame/AI holds 9, mostly BP_Enemy derivatives plus a BP_Turret. The three heaviest by graph size: BP_Player (parent ModularPlayerCharacter, 18 variables, an event graph that drives an ability-input loop), BP_Enemy (a perception-driven state machine that feeds a BehaviorTree), and BP_Turret (a fire-then-cooldown cycle on a timeline). Summaries are reflection reads, no asset is loaded for mutation.
used list_blueprints ×2 → summarize_blueprint ×3
youHand the whole /Game/MyGame/AI folder to the auditor. I want to know which of these override BeginPlay, and whether anyone left dead variables lying around.
aethyr-bp-audit agent Swept all 9. Five override BeginPlay (BP_Enemy and four of its children, each chaining to the parent). The turret does its setup in the construction script instead. Dead weight: BP_Enemy declares LastKnownTarget and bWasAlerted that are written but never read anywhere in its graphs, and BP_Turret has an unused SpinUpCurve. Everything I touched was a read, nothing was modified or saved.
used find_overriders → summarize_blueprint ×9 → list_variables ×9 → get_graph
youBefore I touch BP_Player, how much will move if I change it? Find everything that overrides its core input handler, and what depends on the character itself.
Aethyr · your AI HandleAbilityInput is overridden in 3 Blueprints down the player line. For blast radius: BP_Player is referenced by 12 assets, including /Game/MyGame/Maps/L_Arena, a BP_GameMode that sets it as the default pawn, and two ability Blueprints that cast to it. That's your change surface, all from the reference graph, nothing opened for edit.
used find_overriders → get_referencers

Reads are free and fearless. Every call in this whole walkthrough is read-only, so you can map an unfamiliar project as aggressively as you like. Nothing here can dirty a package, trigger a save, or alter one node.

When you do start editing: the safety net is the same one the rest of the site shows. A ritual previews before it applies, every batch passes a compile gate, and the original .uasset is backed up before the first save, so a bad edit rolls back to exactly what you cloned.

sections.heading: ⑦ Grow a bare stat into a system
sections.html:
BP_Enemy keeps its health in a lone Health float. You want a tidier system around it, without ever leaving the asset half-rewritten.

youBefore we touch anything, what variables does /Game/AethyrSamples/AI/BP_Enemy actually have right now?
Aethyr · your AI Five: Health (float, 100), MaxHealth (float, 100), Speed (float, 300), bIsAlive (bool, true) and LootTable (name, DT_Loot). All editable, none in a category. TakeDamage subtracts from Health and calls Die at zero, but nothing keeps Health under MaxHealth and a big hit leaves it below zero.
used list_variables → get_function
youRight. Tidy it up: rename Health to CurrentHealth, file it and MaxHealth under a Vitals category, and add a Heal(Amount) function that adds to CurrentHealth and clamps it to the [0, MaxHealth] range. And do it as one move, I don't want a half-finished asset.
aethyr-edit · your AI Staged as a single batch, nothing written yet. Let me dry-run it first so you can see exactly what it touches.
used preview_ops
Aethyr · your AI The preview comes back clean: 1 rename (Health → CurrentHealth, the 3 nodes in TakeDamage that use it rewritten), 1 new function (Heal with an Amount input, body adds then clamps to [0, MaxHealth]), and both variables filed under Vitals. No conflicts, no name collisions, no dangling pins.
used rename_variable · add_function → add_function_input → add_node → wire_pins · set_variable_category ×2
youThat's exactly it. Commit it.
aethyr-edit · your AI Applied as one atomic transaction. The rename, the new Heal function, and both category moves landed together. Heal and the renamed TakeDamage compiled clean, so the whole batch held. Had the clamp failed to build, the rename would have reverted with it and you'd be back at the bare float, untouched. Verified after: BP_Enemy is compile-clean, no errors, no warnings.
used apply_ops → compile_function → get_compile_status (needs a live editor)

Why preview first: preview_ops walks the entire batch against the live Blueprint and reports what it would do, the rename count, the new symbols, any collision, without writing a single byte. You approve a plan, not a guess.

All or nothing: apply_ops runs the batch as one transaction behind the compile gate. If the Heal clamp had failed to compile, the rename and the new function roll back with it, so the asset is never stranded between a bare float and a finished system. A backup is written before the first save, either way.

Reads are free, so look first: list_variables never mutates and costs you nothing within a turn. Confirming the starting shape before you plan a change is the cheap habit that makes the expensive step safe.

sections.heading: ⑧ Fork a proven Blueprint into a variant
sections.html:
You have a working BP_Enemy and you want a meaner sibling, BP_EliteEnemy, that shares every line of logic but hits harder.

youMake a new Blueprint called BP_EliteEnemy with the same parent as BP_Enemy. I want a variant, not a fresh actor.
Aethyr · your AI Read /Game/AethyrSamples/AI/BP_Enemy first: its parent is ACharacter. Created BP_EliteEnemy under /Game/MyGame/AI/ on that same parent, so it inherits the identical component skeleton. Empty graphs for now. Compiled clean.
used read_blueprint → create_blueprint
youNow bring the brains across. Same functions as BP_Enemy, wired exactly the same. No hand-copying nodes.
Aethyr · your AI Listed the variables and functions on BP_Enemy: five variables, plus Die and TakeDamage. Declared matching variables and function stubs on the elite, then cloned each graph across whole, so every node, pin default, and wire came over intact, not redrawn. The event graph came too. Re-compiled the elite: clean, zero dangling pins.
used list_variables → list_functions → add_variable ×5 → add_function ×2 → clone_graph ×3 → compile_function
youGood. Now make it elite: 250 health instead of 100, and speed 450 instead of 300. Just the numbers.
Aethyr · your AI Touched only three defaults on the variant: Health 100 → 250, MaxHealth 100 → 250 and Speed 300 → 450. No graph edits, no structural change. Backed up the asset before the first write, then saved as it went.
used set_variable_default ×3 → compile_function
youProve it. I want to see that the only differences from BP_Enemy are those three numbers, nothing structural snuck in.
Aethyr · your AI Ran a structural diff between the two Blueprints. Graphs, functions, components, and interfaces are identical, node for node and wire for wire. The diff reports exactly three deltas, all default-value: Health (100 vs 250), MaxHealth (100 vs 250) and Speed (300 vs 450). Nothing structural drifted. Your variant is a true fork.
used bp_structural_diff

Why clone, not copy: clone_graph moves a graph as one unit, carrying every wire and pin default with it, so the elite's logic is the proven logic, not a re-drawing you have to re-verify. Hand copy-paste is where a missed connection hides.

The diff is your proof: bp_structural_diff is read-only and never touches either asset, so running it as the final step costs nothing and turns "I think they match" into "the only deltas are these two defaults." Reads are cheap within a turn, so verify freely.

Safety net: single writes like these two defaults save as they go, so the backup written before the first save is your way back. Nothing in this story touches your working BP_Enemy, which stays exactly as it was.

sections.heading: ⑨ A designer's balance pass, no editor needed
sections.html:
You suspect a loot drop is overtuned, and you want to reason about it without opening the editor or touching a single asset.

youPull up DT_Loot as a table. I want to eyeball the numbers for anything that looks off.
Aethyr · your AI Read /Game/AethyrSamples/Data/DT_Loot. Row struct S_ItemRow, columns Name, Damage, Weight and Rarity, 5 rows. The dagger, sword, bow and staff sit at weights 40, 30, 20 and 8. Then one outlier: Legendary_Sword sits at 90, more than double the next row. A Legendary item with the highest drop weight in the table reads like a mistake.
used read_data_table
youBefore I judge it, show me how the rows are typed. What does the struct look like?
Aethyr · your AI Read S_ItemRow: Name is a string, Damage a float, Weight an int, and Rarity uses the E_Rarity enum. The rarity labels and the weights agree everywhere except one row. Common sits at 40 and 30, Uncommon at 20, Rare at 8. The Legendary row sits at 90. The number and the label disagree.
used read_struct
youIf I nerf it, who else is affected? Look at what uses that table.
Aethyr · your AI Listed the Blueprints under /Game/AethyrSamples and read their variables. BP_Enemy and BP_Crate each have a LootTable name variable that defaults to DT_Loot. A weight change shifts every drop those two roll. That came from reading variables, not from the reference graph, because a plain name isn't a hard reference.
used list_blueprints → list_variables ×2
youGood. When I do cut its weight, plan the change first so I can see what it touches before anything saves.
Aethyr · your AI Here is the plan, nothing written: one value change to the Legendary_Sword row's Weight, no other rows affected. When you approve, set_data_row_value changes that one field and reports the before and after values so you can check it landed. The table is backed up before its first save. Say the word.
no tool run yet: this is only the plan

Reads are cheap and safe. Every audit step here was a read: the table, the struct, the Blueprint variables. Nothing was loaded for write, nothing was checked out, and no .uasset changed on disk. You can trace a balance question end to end and walk away with the editor still untouched.

When you do decide to act, the same care holds. The plan above was a dry run that wrote nothing, and the real edit only lands after you approve it, with an automatic backup written before the first save. The audit you just did and the edit that follows are two deliberate, separate acts.

sections.heading: ⑩ When a batch goes sideways
sections.html:
A five-step edit trips on step four, and the whole thing rolls back untouched, exactly the safety net you want.

youBuild out /Game/AethyrSamples/AI/BP_Turret: add a TargetActor variable, a Cooldown float, an AcquireTarget function, then wire its found-actor pin into a new SetTargetActor call. Do it as one batch so it's all-or-nothing.
Aethyr · your AI Staged it as a single atomic apply_ops. Steps 1 through 3 applied, but step 4 failed the compile gate, so the whole batch was rejected. The error is pinned to that op: wiring FoundActor (Actor Object Reference) into the NewTarget input (Pawn Object Reference) is a type mismatch, the pins don't connect.
used apply_ops → get_compile_status (needs a live editor)
youSo nothing got written to the asset?
aethyr-triage · your AI Correct, nothing. Atomic means the whole batch lands or none of it does, and step 4 failed, so the save never happened. I re-read BP_Turret to confirm: no TargetActor, no Cooldown, no AcquireTarget on disk. The Blueprint is byte-for-byte what it was before you asked. Reads like that are free inside the turn, so confirming costs nothing.
used read_blueprint → get_dirty_packages (needs a live editor)
youFix the one bad op, then check it before you commit anything.
Aethyr · your AI The fix is to cast first: I retargeted step 4 to feed AcquireTarget's output through a Cast To Pawn node, whose As Pawn pin (Pawn Object Reference) matches SetTargetActor's input. Then I dry-ran the whole five-step batch with preview_ops: it validates clean now, every pin type lines up, nothing touched the asset yet.
used preview_ops
youGood. Apply it for real.
Aethyr · your AI Done. apply_ops ran all five steps and saved. A backup of BP_Turret went to Saved/AethyrBackups/ before the first write, and the final get_compile_status came back clean, zero errors, zero warnings. The variables, the AcquireTarget function, and the cast-and-set wiring are all in.
used apply_ops → get_compile_status

Why this is safe: a batch apply_ops is atomic. Every op runs against an in-memory copy and the result must pass the compile gate before a single byte hits disk. One bad op fails the whole batch, and the on-disk asset stays exactly as it was, no half-written graph to clean up.

The loop that pays off: when a step fails, the error names the offending op and both pin types, so you fix one thing, not the batch. Re-run preview_ops to validate with zero writes, then apply_ops once it's green. The aethyr-triage skill walks this read, fix, re-preview loop, and reads stay cheap the whole way.

sections.heading: ⑪ The boss fight that is too easy
sections.html:
Playtesters beat your final boss in forty seconds. One of them used a pool noodle. Time to find out why BP_Boss is a pushover.

youFind the boss Blueprint and tell me how it handles damage. Playtesters are bored.
Aethyr · your AISearched asset names for "Boss" and got one hit: /Game/AethyrSamples/AI/BP_Boss. Summary of BP_Boss: 3 variables of its own, 1 function, parent BP_Enemy. Before reading the event graph I peeked at it to see how big it is. Nothing much there, and the damage code lives in a function anyway.
used find_asset → summarize_blueprint → peek_graph
youShow me how it takes damage. And is anything else changing its health, or is that the only door?
Aethyr · your AIRead BossTakeDamage: it subtracts the incoming amount from BossHealth and stops there. No zero check, no phases, and ArmorValue is 0 with nothing reading it. Then I searched every graph for nodes that set BossHealth. Only one, inside BossTakeDamage. So your boss has one door and it has no lock. BossHealth and BossMaxHealth both default to 50, which a decent sword clears in a couple of swings.
used get_function → find_node
youMake it 1500 and give it an enrage threshold at 30 percent. Add the variable, then wire up a branch in BossTakeDamage that sets bEnraged when its health drops below it. Preview before you commit.
Aethyr · your AITwo plain writes first: BossHealth and BossMaxHealth defaults 50 to 1500, saved with a backup of the asset before the first save. Then I staged the rest as a batch (a new EnrageThreshold float at 0.3, a new bEnraged bool, a branch node in BossTakeDamage, the wires) and dry-ran it. The preview says every op is valid and it would touch exactly one asset. Apply?
used set_variable_default ×2 → preview_ops
youApply.
Aethyr · your AILanded as one batch behind the compile gate, and BP_Boss compiles clean. The boss now has 1500 health and a mean streak at 30 percent. The pool noodle still does 1 damage. Your playtester has been informed.
used apply_ops → get_compile_status (needs a live editor)

Read small, then bigger: summarize_blueprint and peek_graph tell you how big a thing is for almost nothing. get_function pulls one function body, and find_node searches every graph at once. Open the big payloads only when you know they are worth it.

One write, then a batch: set_variable_default is a single write, so each call saves as it goes (with a backup before the asset's first save). The multi-step part went through apply_ops, which only saves if the whole batch compiles.

sections.heading: ⑫ A loot table that needs rebalancing
sections.html:
Players are drowning in legendary swords. Somebody typed a drop weight wrong, or somebody lied about it. Either way, DT_Loot needs a look.

youWe have a loot DataTable somewhere. Find it and show me the whole thing.
Aethyr · your AIOne DataTable under /Game/AethyrSamples: DT_Loot. Read it: row struct S_ItemRow, columns Name, Damage, Weight and Rarity, 5 rows. The everyday items sit at weights between 8 and 40. Legendary_Sword sits at 90. A legendary dropping more than twice as often as the commonest dagger is, let us say, generous.
used list_data_tables → read_data_table
youDrop the sword to 2. And add a Legendary_Goblet row at weight 1, damage 0, rarity Legendary, so it feels like a trophy.
Aethyr · your AISet the Weight field on Legendary_Sword from 90 to 2. The tool echoes the before and after values, so you can see the coercion landed. Then I added Legendary_Goblet with Weight 1, Damage 0 and Rarity Legendary. The row name was free, so nothing was overwritten. The table was backed up before its first save.
used set_data_row_value → add_data_row
youRead it back. I want to see the final weights.
Aethyr · your AIRe-read the table: 6 rows now, and both legendaries sit far below the commons. Your players will whisper about the sword instead of vacuuming it up.
used read_data_table

Read before you write: read_data_table is the cheap way to orient before you change a row. set_data_row_value takes the new value in its string form and hands back what it replaced. add_data_row refuses to clobber an existing row name unless you pass overwrite:true.

sections.heading: ⑬ The menu typo, the night before the demo
sections.html:
It is 11 pm. The demo is at 9 am. The main menu says "Strat Game". You could fix this in the UMG designer, or you could ask.

you/Game/AethyrSamples/UI/WBP_MainMenu has a typo on the start button. Show me the widget tree first.
Aethyr · your AIRead WBP_MainMenu: the root is a CanvasPanel with a VerticalBox named ButtonColumn holding PlayButton, OptionsButton, and QuitButton. Each button has a TextBlock child. The one under PlayButton is named PlayLabel and it reads "Strat Game".
used read_widget_blueprint
youSet its text to "Start Game". Also add a text block that says "DEMO BUILD" at the top, and hook QuitButton's click to a handler called HandleQuit.
Aethyr · your AISet Text on PlayLabel to "Start Game". Added a TextBlock named DemoBadge under the root and set its Text to "DEMO BUILD". Then I bound OnClicked on QuitButton to HandleQuit. That function did not exist yet, so it was created with the click event's signature, ready for a body.
used set_widget_property → add_widget → set_widget_property → bind_widget_event
youCompile it.
Aethyr · your AICompiled: true. No errors. The typo is gone, the demo badge is in, and HandleQuit is waiting for its "are you sure?" popup. Go to bed.
used compile_widget_blueprint

Under the hood: add_widget, set_widget_property and bind_widget_event are for UMG trees. Blueprint graph nodes still go through add_node. Each of these is a single write, so it saves as it goes, with a backup before the asset's first save.

sections.heading: ⑭ The turret that will not fire
sections.html:
The turret is in the level. It compiles, it is alive, and it does absolutely nothing, with great confidence. Read the turret first. Then take a look at the empty behavior tree next door.

youWhy does /Game/AethyrSamples/AI/BP_Turret never shoot?
Aethyr · your AIRead it. BeginPlay calls Fire, and Fire only prints its line when FireRate is above zero. FireRate defaults to 0.0, so the branch never passes. One very patient turret.
used summarize_blueprint → get_function → list_variables
youSet it to 2. Then show me which behavior trees we have, because the enemy one should be doing something.
Aethyr · your AISet FireRate to 2.0, with a backup before the first save. Found one behavior tree under /Game/AethyrSamples: BT_Enemy. Read it: no nodes yet, linked to the blackboard BB_Enemy, which has three keys. TargetActor (Object, Actor), HomeLocation (Vector) and bCanSeePlayer (Bool).
used set_variable_default → list_behavior_trees → read_behavior_tree
youGive BT_Enemy a start. A Sequence at the root, a Wait of 0.6 seconds under it, and a second short wait after that as a cooldown beat.
Aethyr · your AIAdded a BTComposite_Sequence as the root, then two BTTask_Wait tasks under it. Set the first one's WaitTime to 0.6 and the second one's to 1.5. Then compiled the tree: true.
used add_bt_node ×3 → set_bt_node_property ×2 → compile_behavior_tree

Read before you guess: read_behavior_tree lists every node with its class, kind and parent, plus the linked blackboard and its keys. A zero in a variable and an empty tree both show up in one read. Want to see the turret fire for real? Story ⑮ drives the running editor.

sections.heading: ⑮ Prove it in the running editor
sections.html:
The turret is fixed on paper. Now watch it work. This one needs an editor open on your project, and the Epic bridge also needs Epic's own MCP running inside that editor.

youBefore we start poking things, is my editor even awake?
Aethyr · your AIProbed it. State is healthy, the game thread is responsive, and the route is the live editor. That check does not touch the game thread, so it would also have told us if the editor were paused on a breakpoint.
used health_check
youGreat. Drop a BP_Turret into the level in front of the player start, and slow time down so I can watch it.
Aethyr · your AISpawned /Game/AethyrSamples/AI/BP_Turret.BP_Turret_C at the spot you described. Then sent slomo 0.25 as a console command. The reply says handled: true, so the engine recognized it.
used spawn_actor → console_command (both need a live editor)
youNow press play and tell me what you see.
Aethyr · your AIStarting Play In Editor goes through Epic's bridge. Listed the toolsets the editor currently offers, described the one for editor control to see its functions, and called its play function. Then I asked for the PIE state: is_playing: true. BeginPlay calls Fire on the turret, and with FireRate at 2.0 it prints "Turret fires". Look for that line in the Output Log. Slow motion keeps it nicely watchable.
used epic_list_toolsets → epic_describe_toolset → epic_call_tool → get_pie_state (needs a live editor, and Epic's MCP running in it)
youTake a picture for the team channel.
Aethyr · your AICaptured a screenshot to Saved/turret-slomo.png. This needs a session that can render, so on a headless run it reports captured:false with a note instead.
used take_screenshot (needs a live editor)

Native tool or bridge? Aethyr's own tools handle Blueprint graphs, assets and the common editor actions. Things like Play In Editor, the viewport and selection go through epic_call_tool. You pick a toolset with epic_list_toolsets, learn its functions with epic_describe_toolset, and then call one by its wire name.

Bridged writes follow the same rules: a session started read-only refuses write-shaped bridge calls, just like any other Aethyr write. If the bridge says it is not reachable, its discovery tools tell you what is missing.

sections.heading: ⑯ Lava that glows like a lighthouse
sections.html:
The art director says the lava is "a bit much". Players can see it from orbit. Good news, you do not need to open the material editor.

youList the lava materials under /Game/AethyrSamples/Materials and tell me which knobs are exposed.
Aethyr · your AIFound M_Lava and two instances, MI_Lava_Hot and MI_Lava_Crust. Read the base material's graph: exposed scalars EmissiveStrength and FlowSpeed, and one vector GlowColor. GlowColor times EmissiveStrength feeds the emissive color.
used list_materials → read_material
youWhat is MI_Lava_Hot actually set to?
Aethyr · your AIScalars: EmissiveStrength = 12.0, FlowSpeed = 0.4. Vector GlowColor is a bright orange. Twelve is the problem. That reads straight off the asset, so no open editor needed.
used get_material_instance_params
youDrop the glow to 3. And make me a cooler variant instance of the same material called MI_Lava_Cool.
Aethyr · your AISet the scalar override EmissiveStrength to 3.0 on MI_Lava_Hot. Created MI_Lava_Cool as a new instance parented to M_Lava, ready for its own overrides. The art director has been told the lighthouse is decommissioned.
used set_material_instance_parameter → create_material_instance

Instance versus base: set_material_instance_parameter overrides one parameter on an instance and leaves the parent alone. To change the base material's own default, the tool for that is set_material_parameter.

sections.heading: ⑰ Spring cleaning the Content folder
sections.html:
Your Content browser has duplicate names, a heap of redirectors, and a BP_OldDoor that everyone is afraid of. Tidy it, with a net under you.

youGive me an inventory of /Game/MyGame/Props grouped by folder, and flag anything that looks off.
Aethyr · your AIOne call, whole scope: 212 assets in 9 folders. The flags: 14 redirectors (one broken, pointing at a deleted asset), and a duplicate_name on BP_Barrel, which lives in two folders. It all came from the asset registry, so nothing was loaded.
used list_assets
youFind BP_OldDoor and rename it to BP_WoodenDoor, same folder.
Aethyr · your AIFound it with a name search. Checked what points at it: two levels. Then moved it to the same folder with the new leaf. References in other assets were fixed up, and UE left a redirector behind if it needed one.
used find_asset → get_referencers → move_asset
youDelete the broken barrel while you are at it.
Aethyr · your AITried a plain delete. Refused, because two level assets still reference it, and the refusal handed back their names. I did not force it. Forcing would leave null references in both levels, and nobody wants a level full of invisible barrels. Point those two at the right barrel first, then ask again.
used delete_asset (refused, nothing deleted)

IMPORTANT: delete_asset with force=true deletes anyway and leaves dangling references as nulls. Ask for a force only when you have seen the referencer list and you are sure. It only works on /Game and project-plugin content.

Impact first: get_referencers is a fast registry read, so check what depends on an asset before you move or delete it.

sections.heading: ⑱ Who broke the turret?
sections.html:
Yesterday the turret fired twice a second. Today it fires never. Somebody checked something in. Let us look at the evidence without blaming anyone out loud.

youPull the revision history for /Game/AethyrSamples/AI/BP_Turret. Last few check-ins.
Aethyr · your AIAsked your source-control provider. Newest first: three revisions, with authors, dates and descriptions. The latest is described as "quick tidy" and was submitted this morning. If source control were off, or the asset not tracked, you would get a plain reason instead of an empty list.
used get_asset_history
youLoad the one before that and compare the variables with what we have now.
Aethyr · your AILoaded the previous revision into a temporary package that never gets saved and never lands in /Game. Read the variables from both the old and current versions: FireRate was 2.0 and is now 0.0. Everything else matches. A "quick tidy" with a zero in it.
used load_asset_revision → read_blueprint → read_blueprint
youPut it back, and clean up after yourself.
Aethyr · your AISet FireRate back to 2.0 (with a backup before the first save), then unloaded the temporary revision so its temp file does not hang around. The turret fires. The "quick tidy" author owes you a coffee.
used set_variable_default → unload_packages

Old revisions use the normal read tools: load_asset_revision returns a temp asset path that read_blueprint, summarize_blueprint, get_graph and read_data_table accept as is. When you are done, unload_packages with temp_revisions:true frees it. Story ⑧ shows bp_structural_diff for comparing two Blueprints that both live in the project.

Try it on the sample: a freshly installed BP_Turret has no history yet. Set FireRate to 2.0, submit it, set it back to 0.0, submit again, and you have this story for real.

sections.heading: ⑲ Is the wizard awake? And is the spellbook current?
sections.html:
Tools hang, or answers look stale, or you just want to know if Aethyr is up to date. Two tools cover that.

youAethyr feels slow. Is it me or is it the editor?
Aethyr · your AIChecked. The editor is healthy and the game thread is answering, so it is not stalled on a dialog or a breakpoint. The same report shows update_available: true and names the current version. Want me to look at the update?
used health_check
youYes, show me what an update would do. Do not change anything.
Aethyr · your AIRan the update in preview mode. With no confirm, it only reports what it would do and changes nothing on disk. It would download the matching release, verify it against the published checksums, stage it, and swap it in once every client using the current exe has closed. A failed health check on the new build rolls back to the old one on its own.
used apply_update (preview only)
youLooks fine. Go.
Aethyr · your AIRe-ran it with confirm:true since you said yes. The swap finishes when your MCP clients close. Restart Claude Code afterward to pick up any new skills or changed tool descriptions.
used apply_update (confirmed)

Ask first: your AI should only call apply_update with confirm:true after you say yes. It previews by default. On the Fab build, apply_update is not registered at all because Fab updates the plugin itself. Update through Fab there.
